  band (B2g2+E1u-type combination) that is absent in 1L (Zhang X. 2015, Fig. 12, pp.13 to 14; 1L assignments
  in Table III, p.15). Off resonance (514, 532 nm) the
  spectrum is mainly E' and A1'.
- UV (325 nm) enhances combination modes 750 to 840 cm-1 (Zhang X. 2015, p.15).
- Consequence: peak lists and intensity ratios are only comparable at the same laser line.

## Polarization and substrate
- Backscattering, linear: A1g/A1' appears in XX and vanishes in YX; E2g1/E' is present in both with equal
  intensity (Zhang X. 2015, p.6 to 7, Fig. 3c). Use this to separate overlapping modes.
- Substrate also modulates intensity through interference (Buscema 2014, abstract; Li arXiv:1308.3835).
- Mica has a Bg mode that can overlap A1g (Buscema 2014, p.7).

## Pitfalls and artifacts
- Spectral resolution: Lee 2010 used 2.7 cm-1; the 1L-2L separation step is about 2 cm-1, comparable.
- 3R and 1T polytypes break the 2H rules (see materials.md); check stacking before applying the separation.
- Calibrate with Si (about 520 cm-1) in the same spectrum; report the laser line.
- Doping and strain both move A1': a single spectrum cannot separate all causes; say so.

## What to ask
- Laser wavelength, power at the sample, spot size, objective; was power varied?
- Substrate (SiO2 thickness), suspended or supported, encapsulated (hBN), transferred or as-grown.
- Exfoliated or CVD; age and storage; any gating or illumination history.
- Polarization configuration; temperature and environment (air, vacuum).
- Grating, resolution and calibration reference.

## Reference figures
- Lee 2010, arXiv:1005.2509, Fig. 2a,b: spectra and E2g1/A1g positions vs layer number (514.5 nm).
- Zhang X. 2013, arXiv:1212.6796, Fig. 2: 5L, 6L, bulk spectra incl. low-frequency modes, XX vs YX.
- Zhang X. 2015, arXiv:1502.00701, Fig. 12: resonant (633 nm) spectra of 1, 2, 4, 7L and bulk.
- Conley 2013, arXiv:1305.3880, Fig. 2: E' splitting under uniaxial strain.

caveats: The separation threshold between 3L, 4L and bulk is only about 1 cm-1, comparable to the 2.7 cm-1 resolution and to the strain, doping and substrate effects the same table warns about. D is 'about 4L' by the table, but 5–6L or thicker cannot be ruled out. Do not quote a precise layer number for D or C without AFM or the low-frequency modes.

The monolayer/bilayer assignment of B and A rests on the same Δ ruler. Absolute positions are not a thickness measure. B's E2g1 sits 0.56 cm-1 higher than A's, and C's and D's A1g differ by 0.7 cm-1 (about 0.9 cm-1 in Δ); these differences are of the order of the 2.7 cm-1 resolution and the 0.3 cm-1 calibration scatter, so strain or doping is not demonstrated.

In D, the rl_series output lists two very broad bands at about 321 and 330 cm-1 (FWHM about 35 cm-1, position errors of 16–25 cm-1, height errors larger than the heights). These are fit artifacts from baseline curvature, not Raman bands, and should not be assigned (for example to a 'defect' or 'resonant' mode). In B the 222 cm-1 broad feature was likewise ignored. Flake C has one cosmic-ray spike at 265.1 cm-1, which was removed.

Flake C has low signal to noise (strongest band 19x noise), so weak features, including LA(M), would not be visible, and its Si calibration is only about ±0.3 cm-1. Its Δ does not depend on this, but the absolute positions do.

Intensity ratios are strongly affected by interference in the 285 nm SiO2 and by the laser line. The Si-normalised intensity order agrees with thickness but a flake's absolute intensity should not be used to count layers. Optical contrast differences between the flakes are consistent with different thicknesses; they are not an independent proof.

Laser heating: the power at the sample is unknown. Heating redshifts both modes (about -0.012 to -0.016 cm-1/K) and broadens them, and repeated exposure in air can shift A1g by +1.4 and E2g1 by -1 cm-1 (Bera 2017). A single spot per flake was measured, so heating or photo-modification of the thin flakes (especially B and A) cannot be excluded. Multilayer flakes can be thinned by 10 mW at 514 nm (Castellanos-Gomez 2012).

The low-frequency cutoff at 150 cm-1 hides the shear (about 32 cm-1) and layer-breathing modes, which are the proper layer counters above about 4L. The absence of these modes is not evidence of anything.

Alternative for C and D: a thick-flake spectrum can look the same for any N above about 5L. A flake that looks different in the optical microscope could also differ by substrate region (for example a flake edge on bare SiO2 versus on a thicker underlying flake), so a single spot is not necessarily representative of the whole flake.

Can you extend the range down to below about 50 cm-1? The shear and breathing modes would separate D from C and fix N for N above 4.
How many spots per flake, and did the spectra vary across each flake? Thickness steps and flake edges are common in exfoliated flakes.
Is there AFM, optical contrast or a reflectance measurement for the same flakes? A single height per flake would calibrate the Δ and intensity rulers directly.

structured_output.summary: Layer counts from the E2g1–A1g separation (514.5 nm, 285 nm SiO2/Si, Lee 2010 Fig. 2b): B = 1L (Δ 19.2 cm-1), A = 2L (21.4), D = about 4L (24.3, so 4L to a few more layers), and C = bulk-like (25.1, thicker than about 5L and probably much thicker). Two independent observables agree: the Si 520 cm-1 line is progressively attenuated and the Si-normalised MoS2 signal rises in the order B < A < D < C. The spectra are narrow and clean: E2g1 FWHM is about 2.1 cm-1 in all four flakes, with no LA(M) defect band and no 150–650 cm-1 resonant extras. The flakes are therefore good-quality 2H-MoS2 that differ mainly in thickness. A, B and the 1L/2L split are robust. D versus C, and the exact layer number above 4L, are not fixed by this pair of modes. The 1 cm-1 differences in absolute position between flakes (including the E2g1 that sits 0.5 cm-1 higher in B than in A) must not be read as strain or doping without a more careful look.

caveats: The separation threshold between 3L, 4L and bulk is only about 1 cm-1, comparable to the 2.7 cm-1 resolution and to the strain, doping and substrate effects the same table warns about. D is 'about 4L' by the table, but 5–6L or thicker cannot be ruled out. Do not quote a precise layer number for D or C without AFM or the low-frequency modes.

The monolayer/bilayer assignment of B and A rests on the same Δ ruler. Absolute positions are not a thickness measure. B's E2g1 sits 0.56 cm-1 higher than A's, and C's and D's A1g differ by 0.7 cm-1 (about 0.9 cm-1 in Δ); these differences are of the order of the 2.7 cm-1 resolution and the 0.3 cm-1 calibration scatter, so strain or doping is not demonstrated.

In D, the rl_series output lists two very broad bands at about 321 and 330 cm-1 (FWHM about 35 cm-1, position errors of 16–25 cm-1, height errors larger than the heights). These are fit artifacts from baseline curvature, not Raman bands, and should not be assigned (for example to a 'defect' or 'resonant' mode). In B the 222 cm-1 broad feature was likewise ignored. Flake C has one cosmic-ray spike at 265.1 cm-1, which was removed.

Flake C has low signal to noise (strongest band 19x noise), so weak features, including LA(M), would not be visible, and its Si calibration is only about ±0.3 cm-1. Its Δ does not depend on this, but the absolute positions do.

Intensity ratios are strongly affected by interference in the 285 nm SiO2 and by the laser line. The Si-normalised intensity order agrees with thickness but a flake's absolute intensity should not be used to count layers. Optical contrast differences between the flakes are consistent with different thicknesses; they are not an independent proof.

Laser heating: the power at the sample is unknown. Heating redshifts both modes (about -0.012 to -0.016 cm-1/K) and broadens them, and repeated exposure in air can shift A1g by +1.4 and E2g1 by -1 cm-1 (Bera 2017). A single spot per flake was measured, so heating or photo-modification of the thin flakes (especially B and A) cannot be excluded. Multilayer flakes can be thinned by 10 mW at 514 nm (Castellanos-Gomez 2012).

The low-frequency cutoff at 150 cm-1 hides the shear (about 32 cm-1) and layer-breathing modes, which are the proper layer counters above about 4L. The absence of these modes is not evidence of anything.

Alternative for C and D: a thick-flake spectrum can look the same for any N above about 5L. A flake that looks different in the optical microscope could also differ by substrate region (for example a flake edge on bare SiO2 versus on a thicker underlying flake), so a single spot is not necessarily representative of the whole flake.
questions_for_user: What was the laser power at the sample, and was it varied? Heating and photo-annealing shift the modes by about the size of the differences between flakes.
Can you run a polarized pair (XX/YX)? A1g vanishes in crossed polarization while E2g1 stays, which confirms the mode assignment and would show any overlapping feature.
Can you extend the range down to below about 50 cm-1? The shear and breathing modes would separate D from C and fix N for N above 4.
How many spots per flake, and did the spectra vary across each flake? Thickness steps and flake edges are common in exfoliated flakes.
Is there AFM, optical contrast or a reflectance measurement for the same flakes? A single height per flake would calibrate the Δ and intensity rulers directly.
Were the Si line and the laser line calibrated, and is the 0.7 cm-1 low offset the same on all days? C has no usable Si line.

limits: Layer numbers above 4L (flakes D and C) cannot be fixed from the E2g1–A1g pair; only 'about 4 to a few more' (D) and 'at least about 5L' (C) are supported.

The relation is calibrated for exfoliated 2H-MoS2 on 285 nm SiO2/Si at 514.5 nm, which matches this sample. It does not account for strain, doping or heating, so assignments of 1L/2L carry about ±0.5 cm-1 uncertainty in Δ.
The data cannot separate strain, doping, heating and calibration effects on the 1 cm-1 position differences, because there is a single spectrum per flake, no polarization series and no power series.

The data cannot tell the stacking (2H vs 3R) of A, B and D, because the shear and breathing modes below 150 cm-1 are not covered. The E2g1/A1g pair does not distinguish 2H from 3R bilayers (Ranjuna 2023).
The data cannot give thickness in nm; the thickness of C is only a lower bound from the Si attenuation.

The literature positions in Lee 2010 (bulk E2g1 382.2 cm-1) are on a different calibration from the Si-corrected positions here (bulk E2g1 about 383.0 cm-1), so only differences (Δ) were compared, not absolute positions.
The only literature checks done were against the curated MoS2 note and relations (the Lee 2010 Fig. 2b table); the figures of the cited papers were not independently re-read here.
